summary: Jon Postel's account of the ad hoc Telnet protocol as it was then understood, including the Network Virtual Terminal, with proposed changes. He states plainly that there was no Official Telnet Protocol yet. It was updated by RFC 435.

plainLanguage.summary: A write-up of how terminal sessions over the network worked at the time, with the honest admission that there was no official rulebook yet.

questions: what is the network virtual terminal
subtitle: Jon Postel's candid write-up of the ad hoc Telnet protocol: a virtual terminal, a few control signals and some proposed cuts.

tldr.problem: Every host on the network had different terminals and conventions, and a promised official Telnet specification had not been written. The RFC itself says there is NO Official Telnet Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: It describes the ad hoc protocol: a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) with a printer and keyboard using 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit codes, CR LF as end of line, and control signals numbered 128 and up for things like BREAK and ECHO.
tldr.outcome: It also lists changes proposed by others, such as dropping the ECHO, NOECHO and HIDE YOUR INPUT signals and the data type escapes. RFC 435 is listed as updating this document.

today: The metadata lists no formal status for RFC 318, and it says the document updates RFC 158 and is itself updated by RFC 435. The text describes an ad hoc protocol and states plainly that no official Telnet protocol existed yet.

sections.title: An Admission and a Description
sections.content:
At the October 1971 Network Working Group meeting, Jon Postel promised a document that clearly and succinctly specified the Official Telnet Protocol. He opens by saying this document meets none of that promise: it is neither prompt, clear nor succinct, and there is NO Official Telnet Protocol.

What follows is his understanding of the ad hoc Telnet protocol, taken from RFC 139 and RFC 158 by Tom O'Sullivan. The purpose of Telnet is to give a standard way to connect terminal devices at one site to processes at another. It has three parts: the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP), the Network Virtual Terminal and the Telnet control signals.
sections.plainLanguage: The author says sorry for being late and confusing, and then explains the best version of the rules that people were already using.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) is a bi-directional character device with a printer and a keyboard. Characters are 8-bit codes with no timing characteristics. Codes 0 through 127 are USASCII and codes 128 through 255 are used for special control signals. All code values in the RFC are decimal.

The printer can show all 95 graphics (codes 32 through 126). Of the 33 control codes, only 8 do anything on the printer: NUL (0), BEL (7), BS (8), HT (9), LF (10), VT (11), FF (12) and CR (13). The keyboard can generate all 128 ASCII codes.

The end of a line is the pair CR LF. For a CR that is not part of a line end, the RFC strongly recommends sending CR NUL, so the receiver can hold a CR and look at the next character. The idea behind the NVT is that sites need not keep tables of each other's terminals; the serving site defines how the NVT codes map to its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every computer learning about every other computer's keyboard, everyone pretends to use one imaginary keyboard and screen. Each computer only has to learn how to talk to the imaginary one.

sections.title: Control Signals, Echo and SYNCH
sections.content:
Control signals travel in the character stream as codes 128 and up. BREAK (129) stands for the break, interrupt or attention button of a terminal. ECHO and NO ECHO ask the server to start or stop echoing, or report that it is doing so. By default the using site is assumed to provide echo, and the server never sends ECHO or NO ECHO on its own, except that NO ECHO can end a HIDE YOUR INPUT.

HIDE YOUR INPUT (133) lets a server warn a locally echoing user system that a secret such as a password is coming. The RFC admits it is unclear how much should be hidden, and suggests the server instead send a mask on which the user types.

A BREAK can get stuck behind a clogged data stream. The fix is SYNCH: the user sends the special character, then a DATA MARK in the data stream, and the using site's NCP sends an INS (Interrupt on Send). The server then scans the input for control characters up to the DATA MARK and resumes normal processing.

A minimum implementation may simply ignore and delete all Telnet signals from the other side. A standard implementation must process BREAK, SYNCH, NOP, ECHO and NOECHO.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout stop while someone is already reading a very long list aloud, they might not hear you. SYNCH is like also ringing a bell, so they know to look for your message right away.

sections.title: Proposed Changes
sections.content:
Section IV lists changes that are, in Postel's words, not his own ideas, so the presentation may be faulty. He invites RFCs with better arguments for and against.

  • Delete the ECHO, NOECHO and HIDE YOUR INPUT signals. Servers that do not echo have no use for them, and for servers that do, experience showed echo is best controlled by server commands.
  • Delete all mention of data types. Either the stream is ASCII or it is not Telnet; if the type must change, a command in ASCII could be sent in the stream.
  • Require that the minimum implementation lets the user Telnet send, and the server Telnet correctly process, all the Telnet control signals.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers suggest throwing out a few of the fancy buttons because the computers can handle those jobs another way, and making every computer learn the rest.

items.label: DATA MARK
items.desc: Marks a point in the data stream; used with INS for SYNCH.

items.label: BREAK
items.desc: Break, interrupt or attention; from server to user it is a reverse break.

items.label: NOP
items.desc: No operation; may occur anywhere in the data stream.

items.label: NO ECHO
items.desc: Asks the server not to echo, or says it is not echoing.

items.label: ECHO
items.desc: Asks the server to echo, or says it is echoing.

items.label: Hide your input
items.desc: Server warns a locally echoing user that a secret is coming.
